title: The Woman on the Beast: Babylon Unmasked
summary: One of the seven bowl angels takes John into the wilderness to show him a woman dressed in purple and scarlet, drunk with the blood of the saints, riding a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns. Her name is Babylon the great. The angel explains the vision: the heads are seven mountains and seven kings, the horns are ten kings who serve the beast, the waters are the nations, and in the end the beast and its allies turn on the woman and destroy her, while the Lamb conquers them all.
story: The seventh bowl in chapter 16 ended with the words that great Babylon was remembered before God and made to drink the cup of his wrath. Chapters 17 and 18 now slow down and show that judgment in detail, the way a film might freeze on a single scene. Babylon has been mentioned twice before (14:8 and 16:19), but here she is finally seen. The beast is the same one that rose from the sea in chapter 13, the political power that demands worship. The woman is the city that rides on it, the glittering culture of wealth, pleasure, and seduction that power makes possible. This chapter prepares for three more: the lament over Babylon's fall (chapter 18), the joy of heaven and the coming of the rider on the white horse (chapter 19), and, at the far end of the book, a second woman and a second city, the bride and the new Jerusalem (chapters 21 and 22).
historical:
For John's first readers in the Roman province of Asia (western Turkey today), the clues pointed to one city. Rome was famous as the city built on seven hills, and Roman writers used that description of it often. Rome was the city that ruled over the kings of the earth (verse 18), sitting at the center of a sea-borne trade network that reached from Spain to India. A coin struck under the emperor Vespasian (AD 69 to 79) even pictured the goddess Roma seated on seven hills. Many early Christians used Babylon as a code name for Rome: 1 Peter closes with greetings from “The church in Babylon” (1 Peter 5:13). Old Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 587 or 586 BC; Rome did the same in AD 70. The name fit.

The seven kings of verses 10 and 11 have been counted many ways. Some readers begin with Julius Caesar, others with Augustus; some include the three short-lived emperors of AD 68 and 69 (Galba, Otho, and Vitellius) and some skip them. On one count the sixth king, the one who is, is Nero or Vespasian, which bears on the book's date (set out in the introduction). The eighth king who belongs to the seven and was, and is not, has reminded many interpreters of rumors that Nero, who died in AD 68, would return; Roman historians record pretenders who claimed to be him. Other interpreters think the number seven here, as everywhere in Revelation, signals completeness, so that the seven kings stand for the whole line of worldly empires rather than a list to be calculated.
cultural:
Ancient readers knew the goddess Roma, the personification of the city, worshiped in temples across Asia alongside the emperors. Pergamum, Smyrna, and Ephesus competed for the honor of hosting such temples, because imperial worship was tied to civic pride and trade. John takes that picture of a proud goddess and turns it inside out: she is a prostitute. Her purple and scarlet were the costliest dyes in the ancient world, worn by the rich and powerful. Her golden cup echoes Jeremiah: “Babylon was a gold cup in the hand of the LORD, making the whole earth drunk” (Jeremiah 51:7). The name written on her forehead stands in deliberate contrast with the seal of God on the foreheads of his servants (7:3; 14:1).

In the Old Testament, prostitution is a regular image for idolatry and for the commercial and political compromises that go with it. Isaiah calls Tyre a prostitute for its trade (Isaiah 23:15-18), and Nahum does the same for Nineveh (Nahum 3:4). So the charge here is not first about sexual conduct but about a whole civilization's seduction: the kings and merchants who sell their loyalty for a share of her wealth. The beast with seven heads and ten horns combines features of the four beasts in Daniel 7, especially the fourth, which “had ten horns” (Daniel 7:7).
literary: The chapter has two parts: a vision (verses 1-6) and its interpretation (verses 7-18), the pattern of Daniel 7, where a heavenly figure explains what the prophet has seen. The angel's opening words, “Come, I will show you,” are repeated almost exactly in 21:9, where another bowl angel shows John the bride. The two women are meant to be read side by side: a prostitute and a bride, Babylon and the new Jerusalem, a wilderness and a high mountain. The beast's title, the one that was, and is not, and yet will be, is a dark parody of God's own name in 1:4 and 1:8, the one who is and was and is to come. Even the interpretation stays symbolic, since the explanation itself calls for “a mind with wisdom” (verse 9).

outline.t: The angel's invitation: the judgment of the great prostitute
The woman on the scarlet beast, drunk with the saints' blood
The mystery of the beast that was, and is not
Seven heads: seven mountains and seven kings
Ten horns: kings who make war on the Lamb and lose
The beast turns on the woman, and God's purpose stands

doctrines.note: Babylon is idolatry in its social form: wealth, luxury, and power that ask for devotion and reward those who give it. The chapter shows how glamorous that devotion looks and how it feeds on the blood of those who refuse it.
Even the beast's alliance serves God's purpose: “God has put it into their hearts to carry out His purpose” (verse 17). Evil is real and violent, but it is never in charge, and it destroys itself.
The power that seduces the world is not permanent. The chapter pictures evil turning on evil, the beast devouring the city that rode it, as part of the way God brings judgment.

words.note: Porne, prostitute. The ordinary Greek word for a woman who sells sex, used here as the prophets used it, for a city or people who trade faithfulness for gain. The image points first to idolatry and economic compromise, the selling of loyalty, rather than to private sexual sin.

Musterion, mystery. In the New Testament a mystery is not a puzzle without an answer but something hidden that God now reveals. The name on the woman's forehead is a mystery (verse 5), and the angel promises to tell the mystery of the woman and the beast (verse 7): what she really is, beneath the splendor.

Therion, wild animal or beast. Revelation uses it for the monstrous power of chapter 13 and here for the scarlet beast. It is the opposite of the Lamb: brute force against sacrificial love. Daniel 7 had already pictured empires as beasts rising from the sea.

Oros, mountain or hill. The seven heads are “seven mountains on which the woman sits” (verse 9), which to a first-century reader naturally suggested Rome and its seven hills. In the Old Testament mountains can also stand for kingdoms, which fits the angel's next line about seven kings.

christ: The chapter's one clear view of Christ is verse 14: “the Lamb will triumph over them, because He is Lord of lords and King of kings.” The kings of the earth give their power to the beast; the Lamb conquers by having been slain (5:6-9), and those with him are “called and chosen and faithful.” The contrast runs through the whole book. Babylon is drunk on the blood of the witnesses; the Lamb saves by shedding his own. The title Lord of lords and King of kings, drawn from the Old Testament's praise of God (Deuteronomy 10:17), belongs to the crucified one, and it returns on his robe in 19:16. The chapter also answers Jesus' warning that no one can serve God and wealth (Matthew 6:24) by showing what the service of wealth becomes when it is organized into a civilization.

hard.q: Who is Babylon: ancient Rome, a future city, or something else?
hard.a:
The main schools of interpretation answer differently. Preterist readers (from the Latin for past) see the prophecy fulfilled largely in the first century: Babylon is Rome, or for some, apostate Jerusalem, and the beast is the empire and its emperors. Historicist readers, including many Protestant Reformers, read Revelation as a chart of church history from the apostles to the end, and often identified Babylon with a corrupt church power in their own time. Futurist readers expect Babylon to be a literal city or world system at the end of history, still to appear. Idealist readers see Babylon as a recurring pattern: every culture that makes power and wealth into gods and persecutes the faithful, from ancient Babylon and Rome to any later age.

Many interpreters combine these: the first readers would have recognized Rome, and the vision also describes something larger than Rome that appears again and again. What the text itself makes plain is the character of Babylon rather than a date. Readers are wise to be cautious about naming modern nations, leaders, or institutions as the fulfillment; attempts to do so over the centuries have failed repeatedly, and they tend to point the finger outward when the chapter's call (repeated in 18:4) is for God's people to examine their own compromise.

questions: Babylon looks beautiful, wealthy, and admired. Why do you think the vision makes evil so attractive rather than obviously ugly?
The kings of the earth give their power to the beast willingly. Where do people trade loyalty for comfort or advantage, and where are you tempted to?
The beast ends up destroying the city it carried. What does that suggest about the long-term reliability of power and wealth?
